databases-indexes.tldr:
• B+tree indexes: 3–4 levels cover billions of rows; leaves are linked for range scans.
  • InnoDB clusters rows by primary key; secondary indexes store the PK, so keep PKs small and roughly sequential.
  • Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: equality columns first, then the range or sort column.
  • Covering indexes skip table lookups; functions on columns, implicit casts and leading wildcards defeat indexes.
databases-indexes.body:
An index is a separate, sorted data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Almost every relational database (MySQL InnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) uses a B+tree as the default index.

How a B+tree works

  • Data lives in fixed-size pages (16 KB in InnoDB, 8 KB in PostgreSQL). Internal pages hold keys and child pointers; leaf pages hold the indexed values and are linked to their neighbours, which makes range scans a sequential walk.
  • Fan-out is huge: one 16 KB internal page holds hundreds to a thousand-plus keys. So 3–4 levels index billions of rows, and the top levels stay cached in memory. A point lookup costs ~3–4 page reads, usually only the last one from disk.
  • Keys are kept sorted, so the tree serves =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY and prefix LIKE 'abc%' queries.

Clustered vs secondary indexes in InnoDB — the single most important storage fact for MySQL interviews:

Clustered index (the primary key) Secondary index
Leaf contains the entire row the indexed columns + the primary key
Count per table exactly one (PK, else first NOT NULL UNIQUE, else hidden 6-byte row id) many
Lookup by it one tree walk walk the secondary tree, then walk the clustered tree with the PK (bookmark lookup / "back to table")

Consequences:

  • Keep the primary key small: every secondary index stores a copy of it. A 36-character VARCHAR UUID PK bloats every index.
  • Random primary keys hurt writes: new rows go to random leaf pages, causing page splits, fragmentation and poor cache hit rates. Prefer BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT or time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, Snowflake) stored as BINARY(16)/BIGINT.
  • PostgreSQL is different: tables are unordered heaps and every index (including the PK) points to a tuple location (ctid). CLUSTER reorders once but isn't maintained.

Composite indexes and the leftmost-prefix rule

An index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b within equal a, then c. It can serve:

Predicate Uses index? Why
WHERE a = 1 yes leftmost column
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 yes prefix (a, b)
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c > 5 yes, fully equality, equality, range on the last
WHERE b = 2 no (full index scan at best; MySQL 8 may use skip scan if a has few distinct values) b alone isn't sorted
WHERE a = 1 AND c = 3 partly: seeks on a, filters c b is skipped
WHERE a > 1 AND b = 2 seeks on a only after a range, later columns aren't sorted
WHERE a = 1 ORDER BY b yes, and no sort needed rows for a = 1 are already ordered by b

Ordering rule of thumb: equality columns first, then the range or sort column, highest-selectivity equality columns earlier when it doesn't matter otherwise.

SQL
-- Query: a customer's recent orders with a given status
SELECT id, total, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = 'PAID'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Index that serves the filter AND the sort (no filesort):
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_status_created ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at);

Covering indexes — if the index contains every column the query needs, the database answers from the index alone, skipping the table lookup (Using index in MySQL EXPLAIN, Index Only Scan in PostgreSQL).

SQL
-- Covers the query above completely (InnoDB secondary leaves already include the PK `id`):
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cover ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at, total);

-- PostgreSQL 11+: keep non-search columns out of the tree's internal levels
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cover_pg ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at) INCLUDE (total);

When an index is NOT used (classic gotchas)

SQL
WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-10-01'        -- function on the column: rewrite as a range
WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-02'   -- uses the index

WHERE phone = 9876543210                     -- phone is VARCHAR: implicit cast on every row
WHERE phone = '9876543210'                   -- uses the index

WHERE name LIKE '%kumar'                     -- leading wildcard: no seek possible (use full-text search)
WHERE status = 'A' OR city = 'Pune'          -- OR across different columns: often a full scan (or index merge)
WHERE amount + 10 > 100                      -- expression on the column
WHERE is_deleted = 0                         -- low selectivity: the optimizer prefers a scan

Other index types: hash (Memory engine, PostgreSQL USING HASH: equality only), full-text (inverted index), spatial (R-tree), PostgreSQL GIN (arrays, JSONB, full text), GiST/BRIN (ranges, huge append-only tables), partial indexes in PostgreSQL (WHERE status = 'PENDING'), functional indexes (CREATE INDEX ... ((LOWER(email))) in MySQL 8.0.13+ and PostgreSQL).

The cost of indexes: every INSERT, DELETE and indexed-column UPDATE must maintain each index; more indexes mean slower writes, more memory and more disk. Drop unused ones (sys.schema_unused_indexes in MySQL, pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 in PostgreSQL).

Interview tip when asked "why is this query slow?", talk through: is there an index the predicate can seek on (leftmost prefix, no functions), does it avoid a sort, is it covering, and how selective is it. Then say you'd confirm with EXPLAIN.

databases-explain.tldr:
• Read type, key, rows, filtered and Extra in MySQL; compare estimated vs actual rows in PostgreSQL.
  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows real timings.
  • Find slow queries with the slow log, performance_schema or pg_stat_statements.
  • Use keyset pagination instead of deep OFFSET; select fewer columns; batch round trips.
databases-explain.body:
Never guess at query performance: ask the optimizer for its plan.

MySQL EXPLAIN — the columns that matter

SQL
EXPLAIN SELECT o.id, o.total
FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id = 42 AND o.created_at >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
Column What to look for
type access method, best to worst: system / const (PK or unique lookup) → eq_ref (one row per join row via unique key) → ref (non-unique equality) → range → index (full index scan) → ALL (full table scan)
possible_keys / key candidate indexes vs the one chosen; NULL key = no index used
key_len how many bytes of a composite index are used: tells you how many columns of the prefix matched
rows × filtered estimated rows examined and the % kept after the WHERE; big rows with small output = wasted work
Extra Using index (covering, good) · Using index condition (index condition pushdown) · Using where (filter after reading) · Using filesort (extra sort step) · Using temporary (temp table, often from GROUP BY/DISTINCT)

Plans are trees, executed bottom-up — a typical OLTP join plan:

Read from the leaves: how is each table accessed, how many rows flow up, and where the time goes. The expensive node is usually the one with many rows in, few rows out (a filter the index didn't handle) or a Sort/Hash spilling to disk.

From slow to fast — one query, three indexes

Measure, don't just estimate: EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+, PostgreSQL) actually runs the query and shows real row counts and timings per step.

SQL
-- PostgreSQL
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...;
--  Index Scan using idx_orders_cust_created on orders  (cost=0.43..85.10 rows=20 width=16)
--                                                     (actual time=0.031..0.090 rows=20 loops=1)
--  Buffers: shared hit=24

In PostgreSQL plans, compare estimated rows vs actual rows: a large mismatch means stale statistics (ANALYZE table) or correlated columns (CREATE STATISTICS). Watch for Seq Scan on big tables, Sort with external merge Disk, and nested loops with large outer row counts.

Finding slow queries in production

  • MySQL: slow query log (long_query_time = 0.5), performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest, sys.statement_analysis.
  • PostgreSQL: pg_stat_statements (top queries by total time), auto_explain for plans of slow queries, log_min_duration_statement.
  • Application side: Hibernate statistics, Micrometer timers per repository method, traces showing DB spans.

Optimization playbook

  1. Fix the access path: the right composite or covering index; remove functions on indexed columns.
  2. Fetch less: select only needed columns (no SELECT *), paginate, aggregate in the database instead of in Java.
  3. Fewer round trips: kill N+1 queries (fetch joins, IN batches), use JDBC batching for writes.
  4. Keyset pagination instead of OFFSET for deep pages:
SQL
-- OFFSET reads and throws away 100,000 rows to return 20:
SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

-- Keyset (seek) pagination: start after the last row of the previous page. Constant cost per page.
SELECT id, title, created_at FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId)        -- row-value comparison (MySQL 8 / PostgreSQL)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Needs an index on (created_at, id). The tie-breaker `id` makes the order total.
  1. Rewrite expensive shapes: correlated subqueries into joins, OR into UNION ALL of two indexed queries, NOT IN (subquery) (NULL pitfalls) into NOT EXISTS.
  2. Precompute what is read far more than written: summary tables, materialized views, a cache.
  3. Archive cold data so hot tables and indexes fit in memory.
Java
// Keyset pagination with Spring Data JPA
public interface PostRepository extends JpaRepository<Post, Long> {
    @Query("""
        select p from Post p
        where p.createdAt < :createdAt or (p.createdAt = :createdAt and p.id < :id)
        order by p.createdAt desc, p.id desc
        """)
    List<Post> nextPage(@Param("createdAt") Instant createdAt, @Param("id") long id, Pageable limit);
}
// first page: findTop20ByOrderByCreatedAtDescIdDesc(); next pages: nextPage(last.createdAt, last.id, PageRequest.of(0, 20))
// Spring Data 3.1+ also offers ScrollPosition / Window<T> for keyset scrolling.

Pitfall COUNT(*) for "page 1 of N" on a large InnoDB table is a full index scan every time. Show "next page" links, cache approximate counts, or use estimates (information_schema.tables.table_rows, pg_class.reltuples).

databases-transactions.tldr:
• Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew.
  • MySQL defaults to REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL to READ COMMITTED.
  • InnoDB doesn't detect lost updates; PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ raises serialization errors.
  • Prevent lost updates with atomic UPDATEs, FOR UPDATE, version columns, or stronger isolation plus retry.
databases-transactions.body:
ACID

Letter Guarantee How databases implement it
Atomicity all statements of a transaction take effect, or none undo log (InnoDB), MVCC tuple versions (PostgreSQL)
Consistency constraints and invariants hold after commit constraints, FKs, triggers, and your application logic
Isolation concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work MVCC + locks, per isolation level
Durability committed data survives a crash write-ahead log flushed on commit (redo log / WAL), innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1, synchronous_commit=on

The anomalies, with concrete examples

Anomaly What happens Example
Dirty read T2 reads data T1 hasn't committed; T1 rolls back T2 sees a balance of 0 from a transfer that later failed
Non-repeatable read T1 reads a row twice and gets different values because T2 committed an update in between report shows two different totals for the same account
Phantom read T1 re-runs a range query and sees new rows inserted by T2 COUNT(*) WHERE status='PENDING' changes mid-transaction
Lost update T1 and T2 read the same value, both write back a computed value; one write is lost two requests both read stock = 5, both write 4 (should be 3)
Write skew T1 and T2 read an overlapping set, each updates different rows based on what it read, together breaking an invariant two on-call doctors each check "someone else is on call" and both go off call

Lost update, step by step (the anomaly behind most "the counter is wrong" bugs):

Write skew — two transactions read the same rows, each makes a decision, then write different rows:

Isolation levels (SQL standard) and what they prevent

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable Phantom Default in
READ UNCOMMITTED possible possible possible —
READ COMMITTED prevented possible possible PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server
REPEATABLE READ prevented prevented possible by the standard MySQL InnoDB
SERIALIZABLE prevented prevented prevented —

How the two big engines actually behave (interviewers love this):

  • MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ: plain SELECTs read a consistent snapshot taken at the first read, so non-repeatable reads and phantoms don't appear for snapshot reads. Locking reads (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, UPDATE, DELETE) read the latest committed version and take next-key locks, which block phantom inserts into the scanned range. InnoDB does not detect lost updates: read-then-write in application code can still lose updates.
  • PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ is true snapshot isolation: a concurrent update to a row you then try to update fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update (retry the transaction). Phantoms are prevented. Write skew is still possible.
  • PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): it detects dangerous read/write dependency patterns and aborts one transaction. Expect serialization failures and retry.

Preventing lost updates — the four tools

SQL
-- 1. Atomic update: let the database do the arithmetic (best when possible)
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock >= 1;   -- check affected rows = 1

-- 2. Pessimistic lock: read with intent to update
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE;   -- others block here until we commit
UPDATE products SET stock = 4 WHERE id = 7;
COMMIT;

-- 3. Optimistic lock: version column, retry on conflict
UPDATE products SET stock = 4, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 12;  -- 0 rows -> someone else won

-- 4. Stronger isolation: SERIALIZABLE (or REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL) + retry loop
Java
// Optimistic locking retry in Spring (JPA @Version on the entity)
@Retryable(retryFor = ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class, maxAttempts = 3,
           backoff = @Backoff(delay = 50, multiplier = 2))
@Transactional
public void reserve(long productId, int qty) {
    Product p = products.findById(productId).orElseThrow();
    if (p.getStock() < qty) throw new OutOfStockException(productId);
    p.setStock(p.getStock() - qty);      // flush issues UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=?
}

Preventing write skew: lock the rows the decision depends on (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the set of on-call doctors), materialize the conflict (a row representing the shift that both must update), use a constraint, or use SERIALIZABLE.

Interview tip "Which isolation level do you use?" Good answer: the default (READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL, REPEATABLE READ on MySQL), plus explicit row locks or optimistic versioning exactly where business invariants need them, rather than raising isolation globally.

databases-mvcc.tldr:
• InnoDB keeps old versions in undo logs and reads them through read views; PostgreSQL keeps dead tuples cleaned by VACUUM.
  • Long transactions grow undo history or bloat tables.
  • InnoDB locks index records; next-key locks block phantoms; unindexed updates lock many rows.
  • Avoid deadlocks with consistent order, short transactions, upserts and retries.
databases-mvcc.body:
MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) lets readers and writers not block each other: writers create new versions; readers see the version that was committed as of their snapshot.

InnoDB implementation

The version chain a reader walks

  • Each row carries hidden fields: DB_TRX_ID (last transaction that modified it) and DB_ROLL_PTR (pointer into the undo log with the previous version).
  • A read view (snapshot) records which transactions were active when it was created. Reading a row walks the undo chain back to the newest version visible to the read view.
  • REPEATABLE READ creates the read view at the transaction's first consistent read; READ COMMITTED creates a fresh one for every statement.
  • Old versions are removed by the purge thread once no read view needs them. A long-running transaction keeps undo history alive, so History list length in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS grows and every read slows down.

PostgreSQL implementation

  • An UPDATE writes a new tuple and marks the old one dead (xmin/xmax transaction ids decide visibility). Indexes may need new entries too (unless it's a HOT update).
  • Dead tuples are reclaimed by VACUUM (autovacuum). Long transactions or abandoned replication slots stop vacuum, causing table bloat; very old transaction ids risk wraparound, which autovacuum prevents with aggressive freezing.
InnoDB PostgreSQL
Old versions stored in undo log (separate) the table itself (dead tuples)
Cleanup purge thread VACUUM / autovacuum
Update cost in-place change + undo record new tuple + possibly index entries
Long transactions cause growing history list, slower reads bloat, vacuum can't clean

InnoDB lock types

Lock Locks Taken by
Record lock one index record UPDATE ... WHERE id = 5, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a unique match
Gap lock the gap between index records (no inserts there) range locking reads in REPEATABLE READ
Next-key lock record + the gap before it default for locking reads and updates in REPEATABLE READ: this is what blocks phantoms
Insert intention lock a gap, for an insert at a position INSERT (conflicts with gap locks)
Shared (S) / exclusive (X) read vs write FOR SHARE / FOR UPDATE, writes
Intention locks (IS/IX) table-level markers taken automatically before row locks

Key facts: locks are taken on index records, so an UPDATE whose WHERE can't use an index scans and locks every row it examines (effectively the table). In READ COMMITTED, InnoDB uses mostly record locks without gap locks, which means fewer deadlocks but phantoms are possible for locking reads.

Deadlocks

SQL
-- T1                                        -- T2
BEGIN;                                       BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100          UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 50
  WHERE id = 1;  -- locks row 1                WHERE id = 2;  -- locks row 2
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100          UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 50
  WHERE id = 2;  -- waits for T2               WHERE id = 1;  -- waits for T1 -> DEADLOCK

InnoDB detects the cycle immediately and rolls back the transaction with the smaller undo (ERROR 1213: Deadlock found); PostgreSQL checks after deadlock_timeout (1 s) and aborts one (deadlock detected). Investigate with SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS (LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK) or innodb_print_all_deadlocks=ON.

Avoiding deadlocks

  1. Access rows in a consistent order (e.g. sort account ids before locking) — the same rule as Java lock ordering.
  2. Keep transactions short; no remote calls inside them.
  3. Make sure locking statements use indexes, so they lock few rows.
  4. Avoid gap-lock heavy patterns: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on non-existent keys followed by INSERT from two sessions deadlocks on gap/insert-intention locks; use INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (MySQL) or INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (PostgreSQL) instead.
  5. Retry deadlock victims: they're expected under concurrency, not bugs by themselves.
Java
// Spring: retry transient concurrency failures (deadlock, lock wait timeout, serialization failure)
@Retryable(retryFor = { CannotAcquireLockException.class, PessimisticLockingFailureException.class },
           maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 30, multiplier = 2, random = true))
@Transactional
public void transfer(long from, long to, BigDecimal amount) {
    long first = Math.min(from, to), second = Math.max(from, to);   // consistent lock order
    Account a = accounts.lockById(first);                           // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    Account b = accounts.lockById(second);
    // ... debit / credit
}

Lock wait vs deadlock: a lock wait just blocks until innodb_lock_wait_timeout (50 s default) or lock_timeout (PostgreSQL, disabled by default). Set an application-level statement/lock timeout so a stuck lock fails fast instead of exhausting your connection pool.

databases-schema.tldr:
• Normalize to 3NF by default; denormalize deliberately with a clear owner for each copy.
  • Use surrogate keys, unique constraints on natural keys, and foreign keys unless there's a reason not to.
  • Money as DECIMAL or integer minor units; timestamps in UTC with time zone; UUIDs as binary.
  • Soft deletes need filtered queries and partial unique indexes.
databases-schema.body:
Normalization removes redundancy so each fact is stored once:

A normalized order schema (3NF) with the keys and constraints interviewers expect:

Note the deliberate denormalizations: unit_price_paise on the order line (the product's price changes later, the invoice must not) and total_paise on the order (read on every listing).

Form Rule Violation example
1NF atomic values, no repeating groups phones = '98…, 99…' in one column
2NF 1NF + no attribute depends on part of a composite key order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name) — name depends on product only
3NF 2NF + no attribute depends on another non-key attribute orders(id, customer_id, customer_city) — city depends on the customer
BCNF every determinant is a candidate key rare edge cases with overlapping candidate keys

Denormalize deliberately when reads dominate and joins hurt: store order_total on orders, copy customer_name into an order snapshot (also correct for history: the order should show the name at purchase time), keep counters (comment_count). Each copy needs an owner that keeps it in sync (same transaction, trigger, or an event consumer).

Keys

  • Surrogate keys (BIGINT identity, UUIDv7) are stable and compact; natural keys (email, PAN) change and leak meaning. Put UNIQUE constraints on natural keys anyway.
  • Foreign keys enforce integrity and document relationships; at very high write rates some teams drop them and enforce in code, but that's a trade-off you should state, not a default.
  • Many-to-many needs a join table with a composite PK (user_id, role_id) and an index on the reverse (role_id, user_id) if you query from the other side.

Data types that interviewers check

Data Use Avoid
Money DECIMAL(19,4) or BIGINT minor units (paise) FLOAT/DOUBLE (rounding errors)
Timestamps TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (PostgreSQL), DATETIME(6) storing UTC (MySQL; TIMESTAMP overflows in 2038) local times without zone
Booleans/status BOOLEAN, or a VARCHAR status with a CHECK constraint magic integers without a lookup
IDs (UUID) BINARY(16) (MySQL) / uuid (PostgreSQL) VARCHAR(36)
Semi-structured JSON/JSONB for truly variable attributes, with generated columns or GIN indexes for queried keys JSON for everything (no constraints, hard to query)

Common modelling patterns

SQL
-- Audit columns + optimistic locking on every business table
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id            BIGINT PRIMARY KEY GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,   -- PostgreSQL; MySQL: BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT
    customer_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
    status        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('CREATED','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED')),
    total_paise   BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (total_paise >= 0),
    version       BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    deleted_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NULL                                   -- soft delete marker
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- PostgreSQL partial unique index: "one active subscription per user", ignoring soft-deleted rows
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_active_sub ON subscriptions (user_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

Soft deletes (deleted_at) keep history and allow undo, but every query must filter them (Hibernate 6.4+ @SoftDelete, or @SQLRestriction("deleted_at is null")), unique constraints must ignore them (partial index), and tables grow forever (archive). For GDPR-style erasure you still need hard deletes or anonymization.

Avoid: EAV (entity-attribute-value) tables for core data (impossible to constrain and slow to query); polymorphic FKs (commentable_type, commentable_id) that can't be foreign keys; nullable columns that encode a state machine implicitly.

databases-sqlbasics.tldr:
• Know INNER, LEFT, FULL, CROSS, self, semi and anti joins; WHERE on the right table can turn LEFT into INNER.
  • Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
  • Window functions compute across rows without collapsing them; frames define the rows each aggregate sees.
  • NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing; use NOT EXISTS.
databases-sqlbasics.body:
Join types

Join Returns
INNER JOIN only rows with a match on both sides
LEFT JOIN all left rows; right columns NULL when no match
RIGHT JOIN mirror of LEFT (rarely used; swap the tables instead)
FULL OUTER JOIN all rows from both sides (PostgreSQL; emulate in MySQL with LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN)
CROSS JOIN every combination (Cartesian product)
Self join a table joined to itself (employee → manager)
Semi join EXISTS / IN: "rows that have at least one match", no duplicates
Anti join NOT EXISTS / LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL: "rows with no match"

Pitfall a condition on the right table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'PAID' drops customers without orders. Put the condition in the ON clause to keep them.

Pitfall: NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) returns no rows at all if the subquery yields a single NULL. Use NOT EXISTS.

How joins execute

Algorithm How Good when
Nested loop (with index) for each outer row, index-lookup the inner table small outer side, indexed inner join key (most OLTP joins)
Hash join build a hash table on the smaller input, probe with the other large unindexed equi-joins (PostgreSQL; MySQL 8.0.18+)
Merge join walk two inputs sorted on the join key both inputs already sorted (indexes)

Logical order of a SELECT (why you can't use a column alias in WHERE):

Text
FROM / JOIN  ->  WHERE  ->  GROUP BY  ->  HAVING  ->  window functions  ->  SELECT  ->  DISTINCT  ->  ORDER BY  ->  LIMIT

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

Window functions compute over a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them (unlike GROUP BY):

SQL
SELECT
    name, dept_id, salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)  AS row_num,   -- 1,2,3,4 (ties broken arbitrarily)
    RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)  AS rnk,       -- 1,2,2,4 (gaps after ties)
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)  AS dense_rnk, -- 1,2,2,3 (no gaps)
    SUM(salary)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)                       AS dept_total,
    salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)               AS diff_from_avg,
    LAG(salary)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary)       AS prev_lower_salary
FROM employees;
Function family Examples
Ranking ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE(n), PERCENT_RANK
Offset LAG(col, n), LEAD(col, n), FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE
Aggregate as window SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX with OVER (...)

Frames decide which rows an aggregate window sees: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (running total), ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (7-row moving average). With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes all peers with the same ORDER BY value; use ROWS when duplicates in the ordering column matter.

CTEs (WITH ... AS) name subqueries for readability; WITH RECURSIVE walks hierarchies (org charts, category trees):

SQL
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE id = 7          -- start
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, c.depth + 1
    FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.id = c.manager_id                          -- walk upward
)
SELECT name, depth FROM chain ORDER BY depth;   -- employee 7 and every manager above them

databases-sql.tldr:
• Nth highest: DENSE_RANK (or LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1) wrapped to return NULL when missing.
  • Top N per group: rank with PARTITION BY; one row per group: ROW_NUMBER() = 1.
  • Running totals and growth: SUM() OVER with a frame, LAG().
  • Gaps and islands: date minus row number is constant within a streak.
databases-sql.body:
All queries below run on MySQL 8 and PostgreSQL unless noted, and were verified against a sample dataset. Schema used throughout:

SQL
employees(id, name, salary, dept_id, manager_id)
departments(id, name)
customers(id, name)
orders(id, customer_id, amount, status, created_at)
logins(user_id, login_date)
person(id, email)

1. Second-highest (or Nth-highest) distinct salary — return NULL if it doesn't exist

SQL
-- Window function: N = 2
SELECT (
    SELECT DISTINCT salary
    FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM employees) ranked
    WHERE rnk = 2
) AS second_highest;

-- Without window functions
SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1) AS second_highest;

The outer SELECT (subquery) turns "no rows" into a single NULL row, which is what the classic LeetCode 176/177 problems expect. DENSE_RANK (not RANK/ROW_NUMBER) handles duplicate salaries correctly.

2. Top 3 salaries in each department (LeetCode 185)

SQL
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary
FROM (
    SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employees e
) e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.rnk <= 3
ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC;

3. Latest order per customer (greatest-N-per-group)

SQL
SELECT customer_id, id AS order_id, amount, created_at
FROM (
    SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders o
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
-- PostgreSQL shortcut: SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) * FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC;

4. Employees who earn more than their manager

SQL
SELECT e.name AS employee
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

5. Customers who never placed an order (anti-join)

SQL
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- Equivalent LEFT JOIN form
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

6. Find and delete duplicate emails, keeping the lowest id

SQL
-- Find
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS copies FROM person GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Delete (portable; the derived table avoids MySQL's "can't modify the table you select from" error)
DELETE FROM person
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT keep_id FROM (SELECT MIN(id) AS keep_id FROM person GROUP BY email) keepers);

-- MySQL multi-table form
DELETE p1 FROM person p1 JOIN person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id;

7. Running total of each customer's spending

SQL
SELECT customer_id, created_at, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at, id;

8. Month-over-month revenue growth

SQL
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m') AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue     -- PostgreSQL: to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM')
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'PAID'
    GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m')
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

9. Users who logged in on 3 or more consecutive days (gaps and islands)

The trick: within one streak, login_date - row_number is constant. Group by that value.

SQL
WITH days AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
), grp AS (
    SELECT user_id, login_date,
           DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) DAY) AS island
           -- PostgreSQL: login_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date))::int
    FROM days
)
SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS streak_days
FROM grp
GROUP BY user_id, island
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

10. Department(s) with the highest average salary, including ties

SQL
SELECT department, avg_salary
FROM (
    SELECT d.name AS department, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_salary,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(e.salary) DESC) AS rnk          -- window over an aggregate
    FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
    GROUP BY d.name
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;

11. Pivot: order count by status for each month

SQL
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m') AS month,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'PAID'      THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       COUNT(*)                                             AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY month;
-- PostgreSQL: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'PAID') AS paid

12. Each employee's share of their department's payroll

SQL
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       ROUND(100.0 * salary / SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id), 1) AS pct_of_dept
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept_id, pct_of_dept DESC;

13. Customers whose every order was paid (relational "for all")

SQL
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'PAID' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0;

Interview tip say your approach before typing: "rank within department with DENSE_RANK so ties share a rank, then filter rank ≤ 3". Mention the index that would make it fast, e.g. (dept_id, salary DESC).

databases-replication.tldr:
• MySQL replicates via the binlog (ROW format, GTIDs); semi-sync bounds data loss.
  • PostgreSQL streams WAL; HA uses Patroni or managed services.
  • Handle replication lag with primary reads after writes or waiting for the replica's position.
  • Practice PITR restores; untested backups don't count.

databases-sharding.tldr:
• Partitioning splits a table on one server (pruning, cheap retention); sharding spreads data across servers.
  • Choose a shard key present in most queries, high-cardinality and evenly distributed.
  • Cross-shard queries, transactions, uniqueness and resharding are the hard parts.
  • Use many logical shards on few servers; consider Vitess, Citus or distributed SQL.
databases-sharding.body:
Partitioning splits one table into pieces inside one database server; sharding spreads data across multiple servers.

Table partitioning

SQL
-- MySQL: range partitioning by month (partition key must be part of every unique key, including the PK)
CREATE TABLE events (
    id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
    payload JSON,
    PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (created_at) (
    PARTITION p2026_09 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-10-01'),
    PARTITION p2026_10 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-11-01'),
    PARTITION pmax     VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)
);
-- Dropping a month of data is instant and doesn't bloat: ALTER TABLE events DROP PARTITION p2026_09;

-- PostgreSQL declarative partitioning
CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, payload JSONB) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE TABLE events_2026_10 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01');

Benefits: partition pruning (queries filtered on the key touch only relevant partitions), cheap retention (drop partitions), smaller indexes per partition. It doesn't add write capacity beyond one server.

Sharding strategies

Strategy Mapping Pros Cons
Hash on key shard = hash(user_id) % N (better: consistent hashing or many virtual shards) even spread range queries hit every shard; resharding moves data
Range user_id 1–10M → shard 1 range scans, easy to split hot spots on the newest range
Directory / lookup a mapping table tenant → shard move tenants freely, isolate big tenants extra lookup, the directory is critical
Geo by region data residency, latency uneven load

Choosing the shard key: present in almost every query (so queries hit one shard), high cardinality, evenly distributed, and keeps data that's transacted together on one shard (all of a user's orders with the user). For multi-tenant SaaS, tenant_id is the classic choice.

What gets hard after sharding

  • Cross-shard queries: scatter-gather and merge in the application or a proxy; global sorting and pagination become expensive.
  • Cross-shard transactions: avoid them by design; otherwise Sagas or 2PC.
  • Unique constraints and IDs across shards: globally unique IDs (Snowflake, UUIDv7), uniqueness via a dedicated lookup table.
  • Joins across shards: denormalize, or replicate small reference tables to every shard.
  • Resharding: start with many logical shards (e.g. 1024) mapped onto a few physical servers, and move logical shards when adding hardware, so keys never need rehashing.

Resharding without downtime (the hardest operational part):

Using many logical shards (e.g. 1,024 virtual shards mapped onto 8 physical servers) means resharding is moving whole logical shards between servers — the routing function never changes.

Off-the-shelf options: Vitess (MySQL sharding middleware; YouTube, Slack, GitHub), Citus (PostgreSQL extension), ProxySQL for routing, or distributed SQL databases (CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB, Spanner) that shard and replicate automatically with consensus.

Interview tip before proposing sharding, show you've exhausted cheaper options: indexes, caching, read replicas, vertical scaling, partitioning, archiving cold data, and splitting functionally (separate databases per service).

databases-nosql.tldr:
• Document stores: embed what's read together and bounded; reference unbounded or independently updated data.
  • Cassandra: model one table per query, bound partitions, beware tombstones.
  • DynamoDB: partition + sort keys, GSIs for alternate access, single-table design.
  • Default to relational for transactional business data; use NoSQL for specific access patterns.
databases-nosql.body:
Family Examples Model Strengths Weaknesses
Document MongoDB, Couchbase JSON-like documents flexible schema, nested data in one read cross-document joins and transactions are costlier
Wide-column Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase partitions of sorted rows massive write throughput, multi-DC, linear scale query-first modelling, no joins, limited ad hoc queries
Key-value Redis, DynamoDB key → value / item simplest and fastest access by key everything else must be designed in
Graph Neo4j, Neptune nodes and edges relationship traversals narrower use
Search Elasticsearch, OpenSearch inverted index full-text, faceting not a system of record

MongoDB modelling: embed or reference?

Embed when Reference when
data is read together (order + line items) the related data is large or unbounded (a user's millions of events)
one-to-few, bounded growth many-to-many
the child has no life of its own the child is updated independently and often

Document size limit is 16 MB, so unbounded arrays (comments on a viral post) must be references. Multi-document ACID transactions exist (replica sets since 4.0, sharded clusters since 4.2) but cost more; design so most writes touch one document, which is atomic. Index like relational: compound indexes follow the ESR rule (Equality, Sort, Range).

JavaScript
// Order as one document: one read for the order page, atomic updates of the whole order
{
  "_id": "ord_9f2c",
  "customerId": "cus_42",
  "status": "PAID",
  "items": [ { "sku": "SKU-1", "qty": 2, "pricePaise": 49900 } ],
  "shipping": { "city": "Navi Mumbai", "pin": "400703" },
  "createdAt": { "$date": "2026-10-22T08:30:00Z" }
}
// db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 })   // E, then S/R

Cassandra modelling: start from the queries

Writes are appends (commit log + memtable), which is why Cassandra handles huge write volume; reads may touch several SSTables (Bloom filters skip most), so model tables so each query reads one partition in clustering order.

  • Partition key decides which node stores the data (hash → token ring); clustering columns sort rows within the partition.
  • One table per query pattern; denormalize and write the same data to several tables. No joins, no arbitrary WHERE: queries must specify the partition key (avoid ALLOW FILTERING).
  • Keep partitions bounded (tens of MB): add a time bucket to the partition key for time series.
  • Deletes write tombstones; heavy delete patterns (queues on Cassandra) make reads slow.
  • Tunable consistency per query: QUORUM reads + QUORUM writes give read-your-writes (R + W > RF).
SQL
-- "Latest readings of a sensor for a day" (CQL)
CREATE TABLE readings_by_sensor_day (
    sensor_id  text,
    day        date,
    ts         timestamp,
    value      double,
    PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts)          -- partition: sensor+day; clustered by time
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC);

SELECT ts, value FROM readings_by_sensor_day WHERE sensor_id = 's-17' AND day = '2026-10-22' LIMIT 100;

DynamoDB in one paragraph: items addressed by partition key (+ optional sort key); queries must target one partition key (with sort-key conditions); GSIs provide alternate access patterns (eventually consistent); capacity is per partition, so hot keys throttle. Single-table design stores several entity types in one table with composite keys like PK = CUSTOMER#42, SK = ORDER#2026-10-22#9f2c to fetch a customer and their orders in one query.

Choosing: SQL or NoSQL? Default to a relational database for transactional business data (joins, constraints, ad hoc queries, mature tooling). Reach for NoSQL when a specific access pattern needs it: huge write volume with simple key access (Cassandra/DynamoDB), flexible nested documents read as a whole (MongoDB), or search (Elasticsearch next to the system of record).

databases-pooling.tldr:
• Pool size comes from DB capacity (≈ cores × 2 + disks in total), divided across instances.
  • Set a short connection timeout, max lifetime below infrastructure timeouts, and leak detection.
  • Use PreparedStatements, JDBC batching (rewriteBatchedStatements / reWriteBatchedInserts) and fetch sizes.
  • Pool exhaustion is usually long transactions or slow queries, not a small pool.

databases-migrations.tldr:
• Version schema changes with Flyway or Liquibase.
  • Zero downtime = expand, migrate (backfill in batches), contract over several releases.
  • Use online DDL: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, INSTANT/INPLACE algorithms, gh-ost or pt-osc.
  • Set low lock timeouts; long transactions block DDL and everything queued behind it.
databases-migrations.body:
Version your schema like code with Flyway or Liquibase: migrations live in the repo, run on startup or in CI/CD, and the tool records what's applied in a history table.

Text
src/main/resources/db/migration/
  V1__create_orders.sql
  V2__add_orders_status_index.sql
  V3__add_customer_email.sql
YAML
spring:
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration
    baseline-on-migrate: true      # adopting Flyway on an existing database

The rule for zero downtime: expand, migrate, contract. During a rolling deploy, old and new application versions run at the same time against the same schema, so every schema state must work with both.

Example — renaming orders.amount to total_paise

  1. ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_paise BIGINT NULL;
  2. Release N: write both amount and total_paise; read amount.
  3. Backfill in batches: UPDATE orders SET total_paise = amount WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ? AND total_paise IS NULL; (commit per batch, throttle, watch replica lag).
  4. Release N+1: read total_paise; still write both.
  5. Release N+2: stop writing amount; add NOT NULL once every row is filled.
  6. Release N+3: drop amount.

DDL that bites in production

Change Risk Safer approach
Add column MySQL 8 adds most columns instantly (ALGORITHM=INSTANT); PostgreSQL 11+ adds columns with constant defaults instantly specify the algorithm; avoid volatile defaults
Add index blocks writes in older engines MySQL online DDL (ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE); PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (not inside a transaction)
Change column type full table rewrite under lock new column + backfill + switch (expand/contract)
Add NOT NULL / FK on a big table full scan under lock PostgreSQL: add constraint NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately
Rename / drop column old code still uses it → errors during rollout expand/contract over several releases
Huge table alter (MySQL) long locks, replica lag gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change (shadow table + copy + atomic swap)

Pitfall any DDL waits for a metadata lock behind long-running transactions, and every new query then queues behind the DDL. One idle-in-transaction session can freeze a table during a migration. Set lock_timeout (PostgreSQL) / lock_wait_timeout (MySQL) low for migrations and retry.

qa.q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered (secondary) index?
qa.a: A clustered index determines the physical order of rows and its leaves contain the full rows; in InnoDB it's the primary key and there's exactly one. A secondary index stores the indexed columns plus a pointer to the row (in InnoDB, the primary key value), so a lookup through it needs a second walk of the clustered index unless the index covers the query. PostgreSQL stores rows in an unordered heap and all indexes point to tuple locations.

qa.q: Why might the database not use an index you created?
qa.a: The predicate can't seek on it: a function or arithmetic on the column, an implicit type conversion, a leading % wildcard, an OR across columns, or the query doesn't include the index's leftmost column. Or the optimizer estimates a scan is cheaper because the predicate isn't selective or statistics are stale. Check with EXPLAIN, rewrite the predicate, refresh statistics, or adjust the index.

qa.q: Explain the leftmost-prefix rule for composite indexes.
qa.a: An index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b, then c, so it can be used for predicates on a, (a, b) or (a, b, c), and for ordering by later columns after equality on earlier ones. A query filtering only on b or c can't seek it. After a range condition on a column, later columns can't be used for seeking. Put equality columns first, then the range or sort column.

An index that contains all the columns a query needs (filter, sort and select), so the database answers from the index without touching the table. MySQL shows Using index; PostgreSQL shows an Index Only Scan. It removes the per-row lookup back to the table, which is often the most expensive part.

qa.q: What isolation level does MySQL use by default and how does it prevent phantoms?
qa.a: REPEATABLE READ. Consistent (snapshot) reads see the snapshot from the transaction's first read, so re-running a SELECT returns the same rows. Locking reads and writes take next-key locks (record plus the gap before it) on the index ranges they scan, which blocks other transactions from inserting into those ranges. Lost updates via read-then-write are still possible and need FOR UPDATE, atomic updates or versioning.

qa.q: How do you prevent lost updates?
qa.a: Use an atomic UPDATE with the computation in SQL (stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock >= 1), a pessimistic SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before modifying, optimistic locking with a version column and retry, or a stronger isolation level that detects the conflict (PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE) plus retry.

qa.q: What is MVCC and why is it useful?
qa.a: Multi-version concurrency control keeps multiple versions of a row so readers see a consistent snapshot without taking locks, and writers don't block readers. InnoDB keeps old versions in undo logs and walks them using a read view; PostgreSQL writes new tuple versions and later removes dead ones with VACUUM. Long transactions are its enemy because they keep old versions alive.

qa.q: How would you troubleshoot a deadlock in MySQL?
qa.a: Read SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS (latest detected deadlock) or enable innodb_print_all_deadlocks to see both transactions, the locks held and the locks waited for. Typical fixes: touch rows in a consistent order, make the locking statements use selective indexes, shorten transactions, replace select-then-insert patterns with upserts, and add a retry for deadlock victims.

OFFSET makes the database read and discard all skipped rows, so deep pages get slower linearly, and inserts between requests shift pages (duplicates or gaps). Keyset (seek) pagination remembers the last row's sort key and queries WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) with an index on those columns, so every page costs the same and results are stable. The trade-off is no random jump to page N.

qa.q: How do you size a database connection pool?
qa.a: Start from the database's capacity, not the app's thread count: roughly cores × 2 plus disks for the whole database, divided across all application instances. Keep pools small and fixed, set a short connection timeout so exhaustion fails fast, and monitor pending/active connections. Large instance counts need a server-side pooler such as PgBouncer or ProxySQL.

qa.q: What is replication lag and how do you handle read-your-writes?
qa.a: Replicas apply changes after the primary commits, so a read from a replica right after a write may return old data. Handle it by reading from the primary for a short time after a user's write, routing only lag-tolerant queries to replicas, waiting until the replica has applied the write's GTID or LSN, or returning the written data directly in the response.

Partitioning splits a table into pieces within one database server (pruning, easy retention, smaller indexes). Sharding distributes data across multiple database servers to scale writes and storage beyond one machine, at the cost of cross-shard queries, transactions and resharding complexity.

qa.q: When would you choose Cassandra over MySQL?
qa.a: When the workload is dominated by very high write throughput with simple, known access patterns by key (time series, event logs, messaging), needs multi-datacenter active-active replication and linear horizontal scaling, and can live without joins, ad hoc queries and multi-row transactions. You model tables per query and accept eventual or tunable consistency.

qa.q: How do you change a column type on a huge table without downtime?
qa.a: Expand and contract: add a new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill old rows in throttled batches, switch reads to the new column, stop writing the old one, and drop it in a later release. For MySQL table rebuilds use online tools like gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change; for PostgreSQL use concurrent index builds and NOT VALID constraints validated separately. Keep lock timeouts low.

qa.q: What's the problem with NOT IN and NULLs?
qa.a: x NOT IN (subquery) is true only if x differs from every value; if the subquery returns a NULL, the comparison with NULL is unknown, so the whole predicate is never true and the query returns no rows. NOT EXISTS doesn't have this problem and is usually planned as an efficient anti-join.

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and can't reference aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates like COUNT(*) > 1. Put row-level conditions in WHERE so fewer rows reach the aggregation.

All number rows within a window ordered by some column. ROW_NUMBER gives unique consecutive numbers even for ties; RANK gives ties the same number and leaves gaps after them (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps (1, 2, 2, 3). Use DENSE_RANK for "Nth highest distinct value", ROW_NUMBER for "one row per group".

cheat.databases-cheatsheet:
Indexes: B+trees, clustered vs secondary, composite and covering

  • B+tree indexes: 3–4 levels cover billions of rows; leaves are linked for range scans.
  • InnoDB clusters rows by primary key; secondary indexes store the PK, so keep PKs small and roughly sequential.
  • Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: equality columns first, then the range or sort column.
  • Covering indexes skip table lookups; functions on columns, implicit casts and leading wildcards defeat indexes.

Reading EXPLAIN and optimizing queries

  • Read type, key, rows, filtered and Extra in MySQL; compare estimated vs actual rows in PostgreSQL.
  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows real timings.
  • Find slow queries with the slow log, performance_schema or pg_stat_statements.
  • Use keyset pagination instead of deep OFFSET; select fewer columns; batch round trips.

ACID, isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent

  • Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew.
  • MySQL defaults to REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL to READ COMMITTED.
  • InnoDB doesn't detect lost updates; PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ raises serialization errors.
  • Prevent lost updates with atomic UPDATEs, FOR UPDATE, version columns, or stronger isolation plus retry.

MVCC, locks and deadlocks inside InnoDB and PostgreSQL

  • InnoDB keeps old versions in undo logs and reads them through read views; PostgreSQL keeps dead tuples cleaned by VACUUM.
  • Long transactions grow undo history or bloat tables.
  • InnoDB locks index records; next-key locks block phantoms; unindexed updates lock many rows.
  • Avoid deadlocks with consistent order, short transactions, upserts and retries.

Schema design: normalization, keys, types and soft deletes

  • Normalize to 3NF by default; denormalize deliberately with a clear owner for each copy.
  • Use surrogate keys, unique constraints on natural keys, and foreign keys unless there's a reason not to.
  • Money as DECIMAL or integer minor units; timestamps in UTC with time zone; UUIDs as binary.
  • Soft deletes need filtered queries and partial unique indexes.

Joins, aggregation and window functions explained

  • Know INNER, LEFT, FULL, CROSS, self, semi and anti joins; WHERE on the right table can turn LEFT into INNER.
  • Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
  • Window functions compute across rows without collapsing them; frames define the rows each aggregate sees.
  • NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing; use NOT EXISTS.

SQL interview queries (with tested solutions)

  • Nth highest: DENSE_RANK (or LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1) wrapped to return NULL when missing.
  • Top N per group: rank with PARTITION BY; one row per group: ROW_NUMBER() = 1.
  • Running totals and growth: SUM() OVER with a frame, LAG().
  • Gaps and islands: date minus row number is constant within a streak.

Replication, high availability and backups

  • MySQL replicates via the binlog (ROW format, GTIDs); semi-sync bounds data loss.
  • PostgreSQL streams WAL; HA uses Patroni or managed services.
  • Handle replication lag with primary reads after writes or waiting for the replica's position.
  • Practice PITR restores; untested backups don't count.

Partitioning and sharding relational databases

  • Partitioning splits a table on one server (pruning, cheap retention); sharding spreads data across servers.
  • Choose a shard key present in most queries, high-cardinality and evenly distributed.
  • Cross-shard queries, transactions, uniqueness and resharding are the hard parts.
  • Use many logical shards on few servers; consider Vitess, Citus or distributed SQL.

NoSQL: MongoDB, Cassandra and DynamoDB data modelling

  • Document stores: embed what's read together and bounded; reference unbounded or independently updated data.
  • Cassandra: model one table per query, bound partitions, beware tombstones.
  • DynamoDB: partition + sort keys, GSIs for alternate access, single-table design.
  • Default to relational for transactional business data; use NoSQL for specific access patterns.

Connection pools, JDBC performance and HikariCP

  • Pool size comes from DB capacity (≈ cores × 2 + disks in total), divided across instances.
  • Set a short connection timeout, max lifetime below infrastructure timeouts, and leak detection.
  • Use PreparedStatements, JDBC batching (rewriteBatchedStatements / reWriteBatchedInserts) and fetch sizes.
  • Pool exhaustion is usually long transactions or slow queries, not a small pool.

Schema migrations and zero-downtime changes

  • Version schema changes with Flyway or Liquibase.
  • Zero downtime = expand, migrate (backfill in batches), contract over several releases.
  • Use online DDL: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, INSTANT/INPLACE algorithms, gh-ost or pt-osc.
  • Set low lock timeouts; long transactions block DDL and everything queued behind it.
